meta.title: Who really said "Yes, I Am Drunk, But You Are Ugly. Tomorrow I Will Be Sober, And You Will Still Be Ugly"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Fields. Quote Investigator traces the joke to 1863; the "ugly" wording is an unverified 1946 Churchill anecdote. Fields's 1934 film line said "crazy."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Yes, I Am Drunk, But You Are Ugly. Tomorrow I Will Be Sober, And You Will Still Be Ugly'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous joke documented from 1863, not a W. C. Fields line. His real 1934 version says "crazy" - the "ugly" wording belongs to a disputed Churchill story.

answer.label: Not W. C. Fields — an anonymous 19th-century joke
answer.authorDates: Credited to W. C. Fields (1880–1946) and to Winston Churchill – neither is on record in these words
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces this to a family of anecdotes told with different people in the roles, the earliest version it cites appearing in an 1863 Ohio newspaper. The “ugly” wording belongs to an unverified 1946 story about Winston Churchill and the Labour MP Bessie Braddock; the only version W. C. Fields is actually on record for is a line from the 1934 film It’s a Gift, and in it the insult is “crazy,” not “ugly.”

source.heading: Where the joke actually comes from

docMeta.dt: Earliest full dialogue readable in the original
docMeta.dd: The Story of My Life, vol. 5
Augustus J. C. Hare, 1900 — diary entry dated 16 July 1882, p. 362

source.excerpt: “Do you know who I am?” he said; “I am a Member of Parliament and I am Mr. A. B.” — “I don’t know about that,” said one of the roughs, “but I know that you’re a damned fool.” — “You’re drunk,” said A. B.; “you don’t know what you’re saying.” — “Well, perhaps I am rather drunk to-night,” said the man, “but I shall be sober to-morrow morning; but you’re a damned fool to-night, and you’ll be a damned fool to-morrow morning.”
trail: 1 July 1863 — a filler item in the Urbana Union of Urbana, Ohio gives a drunk’s reply to a temperance lecturer: he will get over being drunk, but the lecturer will never get over being a fool. This is the earliest version Quote Investigator cites ↗.

16 July 1882 — Augustus J. C. Hare’s diary records the full exchange, set outside the House of Commons and told at a house party by Sir Stafford Northcote. It was printed in The Story of My Life, vol. 5, in 1900 — page 362 of the scan ↗.

5 August 1882 — three weeks later the same exchange is already in American newspapers: the Daily Republican-Sentinel of Milwaukee prints a full version on 5 August 1882 (p. 5, col. 2) in which the drunk answers “I shall be sober to-morrow, whereas you will remain the fool you are to-day.” That is eighteen years before Hare’s volume appeared, so 1900 is where the diary telling can first be read in the original — not the joke’s first appearance in print. Quote Investigator ↗ tracks it onward through 1890, 1892, 1904, 1911 and 1932, with the names changing each time.

1934 — in Paramount’s It’s a Gift, W. C. Fields’s character Harold Bissonette is told “You’re drunk” and replies with a crazy version of the gag — the only form of this joke Fields is documented delivering (Quote Investigator ↗).

1946, claimed — the “ugly” wording enters with the Churchill–Bessie Braddock story, sourced to bodyguard Ronald Golding and printed in Langworth’s Churchill by Himself. Langworth accepts the encounter but not its originality, calling it “Churchill editing W. C. Fields” ↗; Churchill’s daughter doubted the story.
source.excerptNote: This is the joke’s skeleton, not the quote as you know it. Hare records it as a story told to a house party by Sir Stafford Northcote about an unnamed MP jostled on his way to the Commons — and the permanent defect is foolishness. Quote Investigator cites an even earlier variant from 1863. The word “ugly” does not enter until the Churchill telling.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for this wording, because no work has ever been shown to contain it. The “ugly” version survives only as reported speech in a disputed anecdote. The passage quoted above, from Hare’s The Story of My Life (1900), is in the public domain in the United States; the nearest genuine Fields wording is dialogue in It’s a Gift (Paramount, 1934), a film that remains in copyright.

author.name: W. C. Fields
author.heading: About W. C. Fields
author.bio: Born William Claude Dukenfield in Darby, Pennsylvania, Fields worked his way from vaudeville juggling to the Ziegfeld Follies and then to Paramount, where he built the screen persona that still carries his name: the muttering, put-upon drunk with a talent for the deflating aside. He often wrote his own material, contributing story credits to his 1930s films under joke pseudonyms — Charles Bogle among them, the name on the story for It’s a Gift. That persona is exactly why lines like this one drift toward him: a boozy, contemptuous put-down sounds like something he would have said, which is a different thing from something he did say.

copyAttribution: Not W. C. Fields. The "drunk / ugly" wording comes from an unverified 1946 anecdote about Winston Churchill and MP Bessie Braddock; Fields's actual line, in the 1934 film It's a Gift, says "crazy," not "ugly." The joke itself is anonymous, documented from 1863. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Almost every element of the popular version is borrowed from somewhere else. Here is what belongs to whom.

items.why: The “ugly” phrasing comes from a claimed 1946 exchange with the Labour MP Bessie Braddock. It rests on the recollection of Ronald Golding, a Scotland Yard detective on Churchill’s protection detail, relayed to the editor Richard Langworth; Churchill’s daughter Lady Soames doubted it. Wikiquote lists it under Disputed ↗.

Fields does deliver a version of the joke — but not this one. In It’s a Gift (1934) his character answers a charge of drunkenness with “Yeah, and you’re crazy, n’ I’ll be sober tomorrow n’ you’ll be crazy for the rest of your life,” as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. The drunk-and-ugly line appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Fields page ↗.
Even within the Churchill telling the target is unstable: Wikiquote notes ↗ that Churchill’s interlocutor “may be given as Lady Astor rather than Braddock.”

Quote Investigator’s chronology runs through an 1863 Ohio filler item, an 1882 House of Commons anecdote, an 1890 Broadway streetcar, an 1892 magazine sketch, and repeated Irish-MP versions in 1904, 1911 and 1932 — all before Fields or Churchill. See the full list ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no first speaker to find. Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that the story “has been told in various permutations for more than a century” and that most of the retellings are fictional — including the ones presented as fact. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why this one keeps changing hands
lead: Some quotations have an author. This one has a shape: you call me drunk, I concede it and point out that my condition is temporary while yours is permanent. Fill in the permanent defect — foolishness, hoggishness, craziness, ugliness — and fill in two names, and you have a joke that has been retold for more than a century. Quote Investigator lays out versions set in an Ohio temperance lecture, a Broadway streetcar, and repeatedly in the lobby of the House of Commons, where the participants change every decade or so.

What makes the modern form so sticky is that the last two names it landed on were unusually good ones. Churchill supplies the wit and the wartime authority; Fields supplies the drinking. Between them they cover the whole joke, which is probably why the internet cannot decide which of them to credit and frequently credits both.
context.detailsSummary: What Fields actually said — and what Churchill supposedly said
detailsBody: In It’s a Gift (Paramount, 1934), Fields plays a grocer named Harold Bissonette. Challenged near the end of the picture with “You’re drunk,” he answers, in Quote Investigator’s transcription, “Yeah, and you’re crazy, n’ I’ll be sober tomorrow n’ you’ll be crazy for the rest of your life.” That is a real, datable Fields performance — but the film’s screenplay is credited to Jack Cunningham, from a story credited to “Charles Bogle,” one of Fields’s pen names, so even there the authorship of the individual gag is not something the credits settle.

The Churchill version is an oral claim. Richard Langworth, the editor of Churchill by Himself, was told by Ronald Golding — a Scotland Yard detective on Churchill’s protection detail — that the exchange with Bessie Braddock happened in 1946 as Churchill left the House of Commons late one night. Churchill’s daughter Lady Soames doubted the story. Langworth himself notes that even if it happened, the retort was not original, and points at the Fields film: “Churchill editing W. C. Fields.”
context.pull: The joke is older than either man. Only the casting keeps getting upgraded.

isBasedOn.name: Filler item giving a drunkard's reply to a temperance lecturer
isBasedOn.description: Earliest documented antecedent, not the source of the quoted wording: the 1863 item's permanent defect is foolishness ("I'm drunk - but I'll get over that pretty soon; but you're a fool - and you'll never get over that"). The "ugly" phrasing is not attested before the disputed 1946 Churchill-Braddock anecdote, and no published work has been shown to contain it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator investigated this exact wording, traced it to a family of anecdotes, cites an 1863 Urbana Union item as the earliest variant, lists 1882/1890/1892/1904/1911/1932 retellings, transcribes the 1934 It's a Gift line as a "crazy" version, reports the 1946 Churchill-Braddock story from Churchill by Himself, and concludes most retellings are fictional.

Page 362 of Augustus J. C. Hare's The Story of My Life, vol. 5 (1900) contains the diary entry dated July 16, 1882 with the full exchange ending "but I shall be sober to-morrow morning; but you're a damned fool to-night, and you'll be a damned fool to-morrow morning."

Wikiquote lists the Bessie Braddock exchange in its Disputed section for Winston Churchill, attributes the claim to bodyguard Ronald Golding via Richard Langworth, notes Lady Soames doubted the story, cites the 1882 antecedent, and says the interlocutor may be given as Lady Astor rather than Braddock.

Richard Langworth names Ronald Golding as a Scotland Yard detective, dates the encounter to 1946, records that Lady Soames doubted it, and identifies the 1934 film It's a Gift as the precedent, concluding "Churchill editing W. C. Fields."

The International Churchill Society bulletin states the encounter occurred late one night in 1946 as Churchill was leaving the House of Commons, that Lady Soames doubted the story, and quotes the W. C. Fields line from the 1934 movie It's a Gift.
Wikiquote's W. C. Fields page contains no occurrence of the words "sober" or "ugly" and no drunk-and-ugly line in any section; its Misattributed section lists other quotations instead.

It's a Gift was released 17 November 1934 by Paramount Pictures, directed by Norman Z. McLeod, screenplay by Jack Cunningham from a story by Charles Bogle (Fields), with W. C. Fields playing Harold Bissonette.

W. C. Fields was born William Claude Dukenfield on 29 January 1880 in Darby, Pennsylvania and died 25 December 1946; the article describes him as an American actor, comedian, juggler and writer and confirms the Charles Bogle pseudonym used on four of his 1930s films.
